title: PhGPO: Pheromone-Guided Policy Optimization for Long-Horizon Tool Planning
claim: Injecting a transition prior distilled from easy successes improves return, success, discovery speed, and gains grow with horizon length.
layout: 4 panels in one row: line curves, line curves, box plot, bar chart
description: A single row of four plots comparing baseline GRPO (blue) against GRPO + Prior (red/orange). Panel (a) shows learning curves of average return against interactions (0–2000) with shaded variance bands, where the red curve rises above the blue. Panel (b) shows success rate against interactions in the same style, with the red curve ending higher. Panel (c) is a box plot with jittered points of steps to first success. GRPO has a median near 620 and GRPO+Prior near 490, with a green '−26%' bracket between them. Panel (d) is a grouped bar chart of success rate at sequence lengths 3, 5 and 7, with green labels +16%, +55% and +278% above the red bars. The consistent blue-versus-red coding guides the eye across the panels.
caption: Two-stage pilot experiment with an explicit transition prior for long-horizon tool planning. We distill cross-trajectory transition memory from verified successful tool-use trajectories in an easier stage, then reuse it as a prior for GRPO optimization. Panels (a,b) show higher average return and success rate under matched interaction budgets, (c) fewer steps to the first successful tool-use trajectory, and (d) larger relative gains with longer trajectories.
abstract: Recent advancements in Large Language Model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in executing complex tasks through tool use. However, long-horizon multi-step tool planning is challenging, because the exploration space suffers from a combinatorial explosion. In this scenario, even when a correct tool-use path is found, it is usually considered an immediate reward for current training, which would not provide any reusable information for subsequent training. In this paper, we argue that historically successful trajectories contain reusable tool-transition patterns, which can be leveraged throughout the whole training process. Inspired by ant colony optimization where historically successful paths can be reflected by the pheromone, we propose Pheromone-Guided Policy Optimization (PhGPO), which learns a trajectory-based transition pattern (i.e., pheromone) from historical trajectories and then uses the learned pheromone to guide policy optimization. This learned pheromone provides explicit and reusable guidance that steers policy optimization toward historically successful tool transitions, thereby improving long-horizon tool planning. Comprehensive experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed PhGPO.
